 Order
This criminal revision petition has been filed challenging the conviction and sentence in a prosecution under Section 498A of the IPC.

2. The petitioner faced trial for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 of the IPC before the Assistant Sessions Court, Thiruvalla (for short, the trial court) in S.C.No.66/1995.
3.

The prosecution case in short is as follows:
The deceased Mery Thomas @ Moji was married to the petitioner on 4.6.1981.
After the marriage, she was residing at the matrimonial home at Eettichuvadu, Ranni.
Besides her and her husband, the petitioner and his father along with the 2 nd wife was also staying in that house.
In the wedlock, three children namely Bimji, Timji and Tomji were born.
The petitioner was a habitual drunkard and was a man of loose morals.
He was employed abroad.
He lost the job and returned to the native home.
He treated Mery Thomas @ Moji cruelly.
He developed illicit relationships with other women.
He had developed illicit intimacy with one Ammini who was working 2025:KER:74407 as aya of the nursery school run by him.
When this was questioned by Mery Thomas @ Moji, she was beaten by the petitioner.
He abetted her to commit suicide.

As a result, in the night between 4.11.1992 and 5.11.1992, she committed suicide by jumping into the well in her residential compound in Angadi muri at Angadi Village along with her three minor children.
Thus, the petitioner committed the offences as alleged.
4. Before the trial court, PW1 to PW28 were examined and Exts.P1 to P34 were marked on the side of the prosecution.
No defence evidence was adduced.
MO1 to MO8 were identified.
Exts.X1 to X3 were marked as court exhibits.

After trial, the trial court found the petitioner guilty for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 of the IPC and he was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of 10,000/- under Section 498A of the IPC, in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for seven years and to pay a fine of 50,000/-, in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for two years under Section 306 of the IPC.
The petitioner challenged the conviction and sentence of the trial court before the Sessions Court, Pathanamthitta (for short, the appellate 2025:KER:74407 court) in Crl.A.No.88/1996.
The appellate court set aside the conviction and sentence under Section 306 of the IPC and confirmed the conviction and sentence under Section 498A of the IPC.
This revision petition has been filed challenging the judgments of the trial court as well as the appellate court.
5. During the pendency of this revision petition, the revision petitioner died.
No legal heirs of the revision petitioner have come forward to prosecute the revision petition.

The Supreme Court in Pranab Kumar Mitra v. State of W.B. [1959 KHC 463] has held that on the death of the revision petitioner during the pendency of the revision filed under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the revision shall not be abated and the revisional court has the power to examine the correctness of the conviction and sentence.

P.S.Jayaprakash and Another [2009 (3) KHC 67], following the decision of the Supreme Court in Pranab Kumar Mitra (supra), held that on the death of the revision petitioner after filing of revision before the High Court invoking Sections 397 and 401 of Cr.P.C., the revision will not be abated and the High Court is bound to dispose of the revision on merits in accordance with law.

sentences.text: It was further held that even though 2025:KER:74407 the legal heirs have not come forward to pursue the revision, the jurisdiction of the High Court to decide the revision, after it has been taken on file, on its merits does not cease.
6. I have perused the entire records and heard Sri.E.C.Bineesh, the learned Senior Public Prosecutor.

7. Though the trial court found that the petitioner had committed the offence under Section 306 of the IPC, the appellate court reversed the finding, holding that there is no evidence to prove the offence under Section 306 of the IPC.

However, the trial court as well as the appellate court concurrently found that there are sufficient evidence on record to prove that the petitioner had committed the offence under Section 498A of the IPC.
8. The deceased was the wife of the petitioner.
PW2 is the father, PW3 is the mother, PW4 is the brother and PW5 is the sister-in-law of the deceased.
They had supported the prosecution case.
PW2, PW3, PW4 and PW5 deposed that the deceased was subjected to cruelty both physically and mentally by the petitioner demanding more dowry.
Both the trial court as well as the appellate court believed their evidence so far as Section 498A of IPC is concerned.
I see no reason to take a different view in this revision petition.
It is settled that the jurisdiction of the High Court in revision is severely restricted and it cannot embark upon re- appreciation of evidence.
I have carefully gone through the entire records, evidence, proceedings and the judgments of the trial court as well as the appellate court.
I find no impropriety or illegality therein warranting interference under the exercise of revisional powers vested with this court.
There is no merit in the revision petition.
Accordingly, it is dismissed.
Since the petitioner is no more, the substantive sentence of imprisonment has practically become inoperative.
The fine amount shall be realised in accordance with law.
